title.text: A Castle Fit for a Vampire

textContent.text: Sitting high atop a rocky mountain in the Transylvania region of Romania, Bran Castle offers spectacular views of the rolling hills, dense forests, and flowing river below it. The castle's imposing stone walls, narrow corridors, and hidden rooms create an atmosphere of medieval mystery, captivating the imagination of all who enter. Yet its striking appearance is only the beginning—the castle's long history and the legends woven around it are equally intriguing.

Among the most enduring of these legends is the belief that Bran Castle served as the inspiration for the fictional lair of Count Dracula, the title character in Bram Stoker's 1897 vampire novel. Despite its fame as "Dracula's Castle," however, there is no historical evidence to suggest that Stoker knew of Bran Castle or even visited Transylvania. Another legend has it that Stoker based the character Dracula on a real-life medieval prince named Vlad Drăculea, who ruled an area near Bran. No one knows for certain if Vlad Drăculea had any association with Bran Castle. Nevertheless, the castle's tenuous connection to the Dracula myth has persisted, continuing to spark curiosity despite the lack of historical evidence.

The true history of Bran Castle, though, is just as fascinating as the legends that surround it. In the Middle Ages, the town of Bran occupied a key position along a trade route through the Carpathian Mountains. This brought commerce to the region but also hostile invaders. Bran Castle was initially built as a fortress to defend against these invaders and remained an important stronghold for several centuries. However, as political boundaries shifted and military needs evolved, the castle's purpose changed as well. In the eighteenth century, it served the region as a customs post where goods were inspected as they passed between Transylvania and neighboring Wallachia. In the nineteenth century, it operated as a post office and as a quarantine station for travelers arriving from regions affected by disease.

One of the most notable periods in the castle's history began in 1920, when it was gifted by local citizens to Queen Marie of Romania in gratitude for her humanitarian and diplomatic efforts during World War I. By that time, the castle had been damaged by centuries of sieges, storms, and neglect. However, Queen Marie cherished the castle as a place of beauty and retreat, and she undertook extensive renovations to restore its former glory. While carefully maintaining the castle's original architecture, she decorated it with a blend of treasures from around the world and transformed it into a comfortable and elegant residence. She also ordered the construction of a power plant to provide electricity to the castle and the surrounding towns of Bran, Simon, and Moieciu.

Bran Castle remained in Queen Marie's family until the monarchy was abolished in 1948. The Communist government took control of the property and in 1956, opened the castle to the public as a museum dedicated to Romania's medieval heritage. Its rooms and halls were transformed into exhibition spaces featuring medieval weapons, antique furniture, and regional works of art. Today, the castle still operates as a Romanian history museum but has added exhibits on the castle's former residents and the folklore that links the site to the Dracula story. In this way, the castle preserves the legacy of its many eras, offering visitors a vivid glimpse into the history and legends that surround it.

textContent.text: Straddling the equator, the Maldives is a captivating island nation nestled in the azure waters of the Indian Ocean. This tropical paradise boasts around twelve hundred coral islands, each offering its own slice of idyllic beauty. Among these is Vaadhoo Island, renowned for one of the most mesmerizing natural wonders on Earth: the Sea of Stars.

On warm nights, the shoreline of Vaadhoo Island sometimes comes to life with glowing lights that make it seem as though stars are floating on the ocean's surface. This entrancing display is caused by clumps of tiny plankton that are capable of emitting light similar to the glow of a firefly. The first sparks usually begin at twilight and continue to grow as darkness falls, until the coast transforms into a glowing wonderland. The shimmering glow is triggered by movement—waves crashing on the shore, fish swimming near the beach, and even footsteps across the wet sand.

The science behind the Sea of Stars is as fascinating as the spectacle itself. The magical glow comes from single-celled plant-like organisms called dinoflagellates. When one of these cells is bumped or disturbed, special enzymes inside it react with oxygen, and this chemical reaction produces light, causing the tiny cell to faintly glow. When millions of these tiny cells jostle around together, they create a brilliant light show, a behavior that scientists believe may have evolved as a defense mechanism meant to deter predators.

Large bioluminescent displays like the Sea of Stars are not exclusive to Vaadhoo Island. Many waters around the world contain similar organisms, including beaches in Puerto Rico, India, and California, but the intensity of its occurrence here makes it particularly remarkable. The warm waters surrounding the Maldives provide an ideal environment for glowing dinoflagellates to thrive and come together in huge groups.

Photographs and videos of the Sea of Stars have captivated people around the world, inspiring many to try to see the spectacle in person. But it isn't as easy as it sounds. Witnessing the lightshow firsthand requires a combination of luck and good timing. First, it must be very dark; the plankton do not emit light during the day, and too much artificial lighting can overpower their faint glimmer. Second, it must be the right time of year. The dinoflagellate population proliferates during warmer months, spreading throughout the water. With the plankton present in far greater concentrations, visitors who arrive between late summer and early autumn have the best chance of experiencing the stunning light. However, even during this optimal time and under the darkest conditions, the Sea of Stars doesn't always appear. The amount of plankton in the water varies from night to night, and sometimes visitors leave disappointed.
For those lucky enough to behold it, however, this bioluminescent display captures nature's stunning artistry, making it hard to tell where the night sky ends and the ocean begins.

textContent.text: Straddling the equator, the Maldives is a captivating island nation nestled in the azure waters of the Indian Ocean. This tropical paradise boasts around twelve hundred coral islands, each offering its own slice of idyllic beauty. Among these is Vaadhoo Island, renowned for one of the most mesmerizing natural wonders on Earth: the Sea of Stars.

On warm nights, the shoreline of Vaadhoo Island sometimes comes to life with glowing lights that make it seem as though stars are floating on the ocean's surface. This entrancing display is caused by clumps of tiny plankton that are capable of emitting light similar to the glow of a firefly. The first sparks usually begin at twilight and continue to grow as darkness falls, until the coast transforms into a glowing wonderland. The shimmering glow is triggered by movement—waves crashing on the shore, fish swimming near the beach, and even footsteps across the wet sand.

The science behind the Sea of Stars is as fascinating as the spectacle itself. The magical glow comes from single-celled plant-like organisms called dinoflagellates. When one of these cells is bumped or disturbed, special enzymes inside it react with oxygen, and this chemical reaction produces light, causing the tiny cell to faintly glow. When millions of these tiny cells jostle around together, they create a brilliant light show, a behavior that scientists believe may have evolved as a defense mechanism meant to deter predators.

Large bioluminescent displays like the Sea of Stars are not exclusive to Vaadhoo Island. Many waters around the world contain similar organisms, including beaches in Puerto Rico, India, and California, but the intensity of its occurrence here makes it particularly remarkable. The warm waters surrounding the Maldives provide an ideal environment for glowing dinoflagellates to thrive and come together in huge groups.

textContent.text: The North African country of Morocco stretches from the vast Sahara Desert in the south to the breezy Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts in the north. Between these desert dunes and ocean waves, at the foot of the majestic Atlas Mountains, lies the city of Marrakesh. Established in the eleventh century, Marrakesh quickly became a key stop along the trans-Saharan trading route and grew into a bustling economic and cultural hub. Today, the city retains its original energy and influence, rich in both modern and traditional sights, sounds, and activities.

pieces.text: Marrakesh's modern districts are known for fine art, gourmet dining, and elegant spas. However, the city's traditional charm is best found in the

, its ancient core. Common in many North African cities, medinas are historic town centers that mark the area where the city was first established. These areas retain their ancient architecture, with narrow, winding streets and tightly clustered buildings that house shops, homes, and places of worship. Marrakesh's medina is encircled by twelve miles of ramparts nearly thirty feet high and six feet thick. Constructed hundreds of years ago during a time of regional conflict, these walls were built using a rose-colored clay, giving Marrakesh its nickname, the Red City.

At the heart of the Marrakesh medina is Jemaa el-Fna, a lively open-air plaza that has been the center of shopping, social activity, and cultural expression since the city's founding. Each morning, the square fills with orange juice vendors and small carts and stalls offering quick snacks and simple goods. As the day progresses, more stands appear. Colorfully dressed water vendors with wide red hats and necklaces of clanging metal cups roam the square, their goatskin packs swinging as they wander amid carts and motorcycles. Performers gradually gather, showcasing Morocco's rich cultural heritage: storytellers entertain crowds with ancient tales and henna artists create intricate temporary tattoos. Dancers spin to the rhythm of drums, and musicians play traditional Moroccan instruments like the
, a three-stringed instrument similar to a guitar. By nightfall, magicians, acrobats, comedians, and preachers have filled the plaza, transforming it into a spectacle of sight and sound.
The Jemaa el-Fna also serves as the main entrance to the

, a crowded maze of colorful market stalls that wind their way deep into the medina. The vendors cater to locals and tourists alike, offering sundry goods for daily living as well as souvenirs. Bins of fragrant spices stand near hand-crafted leather bags and hammered brass jewelry. Stalls filled with handwoven carpets, lanterns, cashmere wraps, and stacks of pottery stretch as far as the eye can see.

textContent.text: These unique traditions, and the culture behind them, have been passed down through generations and preserved as part of the rich history of Marrakesh's medina. In fact, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) has designated the medina as a World Heritage Site, a title given to places recognized for their outstanding cultural or historical importance. With its bustling souks, centuries-old architecture, and lively public spaces, the medina is both an enduring reminder of Morocco's past and a vital hub for present-day commerce and community life.

textContent.text: The North African country of Morocco stretches from the vast Sahara Desert in the south to the breezy Atlantic and Mediterranean coasts in the north. Between these desert dunes and ocean waves, at the foot of the majestic Atlas Mountains, lies the city of Marrakesh. Established in the eleventh century, Marrakesh quickly became a key stop along the trans-Saharan trading route and grew into a bustling economic and cultural hub. Today, the city retains its original energy and influence, rich in both modern and traditional sights, sounds, and activities.

pieces.text: Marrakesh's modern districts are known for fine art, gourmet dining, and elegant spas. However, the city's traditional charm is best found in the

, its ancient core. Common in many North African cities, medinas are historic town centers that mark the area where the city was first established. These areas retain their ancient architecture, with narrow, winding streets and tightly clustered buildings that house shops, homes, and places of worship. Marrakesh's medina is encircled by twelve miles of ramparts nearly thirty feet high and six feet thick. Constructed hundreds of years ago during a time of regional conflict, these walls were built using a rose-colored clay, giving Marrakesh its nickname, the Red City.

At the heart of the Marrakesh medina is Jemaa el-Fna, a lively open-air plaza that has been the center of shopping, social activity, and cultural expression since the city's founding. Each morning, the square fills with orange juice vendors and small carts and stalls offering quick snacks and simple goods. As the day progresses, more stands appear.

content.text: Colorfully dressed water vendors with wide red hats and necklaces of clanging metal cups roam the square, their goatskin packs swinging as they wander amid carts and motorcycles.

pieces.text: Performers gradually gather, showcasing Morocco's rich cultural heritage: storytellers entertain crowds with ancient tales and henna artists create intricate temporary tattoos. Dancers spin to the rhythm of drums, and musicians play traditional Moroccan instruments like the
, a three-stringed instrument similar to a guitar. By nightfall, magicians, acrobats, comedians, and preachers have filled the plaza, transforming it into a spectacle of sight and sound.
The Jemaa el-Fna also serves as the main entrance to the

, a crowded maze of colorful market stalls that wind their way deep into the medina. The vendors cater to locals and tourists alike, offering sundry goods for daily living as well as souvenirs. Bins of fragrant spices stand near hand-crafted leather bags and hammered brass jewelry. Stalls filled with handwoven carpets, lanterns, cashmere wraps, and stacks of pottery stretch as far as the eye can see.

textContent.text: These unique traditions, and the culture behind them, have been passed down through generations and preserved as part of the rich history of Marrakesh's medina. In fact, the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) has designated the medina as a World Heritage Site, a title given to places recognized for their outstanding cultural or historical importance. With its bustling souks, centuries-old architecture, and lively public spaces, the medina is both an enduring reminder of Morocco's past and a vital hub for present-day commerce and community life.

title.text: The world's largest salt flat, Salar de Uyuni

textContent.text: Salar de Uyuni, nestled high in the mountains of Bolivia in South America, is not just the largest salt flat in the world—it is a vast, otherworldly landscape shaped by powerful geological forces. Covering more than four thousand square miles, the salt flat is so broad and so reflective that astronauts can see it from space.

The story of Salar de Uyuni began tens of thousands of years ago, when several very large lakes covered this part of the Andes mountains. As the Andes continued to rise, the region became cut off from normal drainage routes. Water could enter the basin, but it had no way to flow out. Over long periods of time, the climate changed, causing the lakes to expand and shrink, again and again. Each time water evaporated, it left behind layers of minerals—mostly salt—on the bottom of the basin. After many cycles of filling and drying, a thick crust of salt slowly formed across the surface. This is the huge white salt flat we see today.

During the dry season, many of the processes that built the salt flat become visible. The crust heats up during the day and cools quickly at night. This daily change causes the salt to crack in repeating hexagon shapes. These connected shapes spread in every direction and create one of the most recognizable patterns in nature. The basin is also extremely level—its elevation changes only a few inches across many miles—so the geometric designs stand out even more against the white ground.

The landscape changes again when the rainy season arrives. Because the basin is flat and the ground does not absorb water well, rain collects in a thin layer on top of the salt. This shallow water reflects the sky so clearly that the salt flat and the clouds seem to blend into a single image. It is because of this annual transformation that some refer to Salar de Uyuni as the world's largest natural mirror.

The region's long geological past also produced an important resource under the crust: lithium-rich brine. Lithium comes from volcanic rocks in the nearby Andes. Over time, rain and runoff carried small amounts of lithium into the basin. Because the basin has no natural exit, this silvery-white metal stayed trapped and became more concentrated. Today, Salar de Uyuni holds one of the largest known supplies of lithium, which is used in batteries for laptops, smartphones, and electric cars.

This mineral wealth has influenced local communities for many years. People have harvested salt from the area for a long time, but the discovery of large lithium deposits created new interest in mining. Lithium extraction has brought jobs and investment to nearby towns, giving families more ways to earn money and playing an increasingly important role in the region's future.

Tourism also plays a major role in the local economy. Visitors travel from around the world to see the mirror-like surface in the rainy season and the patterned crust in the dry months. During the dry season, the flat and empty horizon makes it easy to create whimsical perspective photos. By placing people or objects at different distances, visitors can make it look as though someone is standing on a friend's hand or being chased by a tiny toy dinosaur. These fun illusions have become part of Salar de Uyuni's appeal. They remind visitors that the region's unique geology shapes far more than its surface. It continues to guide how the land is used, admired, and enjoyed.

title.text: The world's largest salt flat, Salar de Uyuni

textContent.text: Salar de Uyuni, nestled high in the mountains of Bolivia in South America, is not just the largest salt flat in the world—it is a vast, otherworldly landscape shaped by powerful geological forces. Covering more than four thousand square miles, the salt flat is so broad and so reflective that astronauts can see it from space.

The story of Salar de Uyuni began tens of thousands of years ago, when several very large lakes covered this part of the Andes mountains. As the Andes continued to rise, the region became cut off from normal drainage routes. Water could enter the basin, but it had no way to flow out. Over long periods of time, the climate changed, causing the lakes to expand and shrink, again and again. Each time water evaporated, it left behind layers of minerals—mostly salt—on the bottom of the basin. After many cycles of filling and drying, a thick crust of salt slowly formed across the surface. This is the huge white salt flat we see today.

During the dry season, many of the processes that built the salt flat become visible. The crust heats up during the day and cools quickly at night. This daily change causes the salt to crack in repeating hexagon shapes. These connected shapes spread in every direction and create one of the most recognizable patterns in nature. The basin is also extremely level—its elevation changes only a few inches across many miles—so the geometric designs stand out even more against the white ground.

The landscape changes again when the rainy season arrives. Because the basin is flat and the ground does not absorb water well, rain collects in a thin layer on top of the salt. This shallow water reflects the sky so clearly that the salt flat and the clouds seem to blend into a single image. It is because of this annual transformation that some refer to Salar de Uyuni as the world's largest natural mirror.

The region's long geological past also produced an important resource under the crust: lithium-rich brine. Lithium comes from volcanic rocks in the nearby Andes. Over time, rain and runoff carried small amounts of lithium into the basin. Because the basin has no natural exit, this silvery-white metal stayed trapped and became more concentrated. Today, Salar de Uyuni holds one of the largest known supplies of lithium, which is used in batteries for laptops, smartphones, and electric cars.

This mineral wealth has influenced local communities for many years. People have harvested salt from the area for a long time, but the discovery of large lithium deposits created new interest in mining. Lithium extraction has brought jobs and investment to nearby towns, giving families more ways to earn money and playing an increasingly important role in the region's future.

Tourism also plays a major role in the local economy. Visitors travel from around the world to see the mirror-like surface in the rainy season and the patterned crust in the dry months. During the dry season, the flat and empty horizon makes it easy to create whimsical perspective photos. By placing people or objects at different distances, visitors can make it look as though someone is standing on a friend's hand or being chased by a tiny toy dinosaur. These fun illusions have become part of Salar de Uyuni's appeal. They remind visitors that the region's unique geology shapes far more than its surface. It continues to guide how the land is used, admired, and enjoyed.

textContent.text: Since ancient times, people around the world have used plants to treat illnesses and support human health. However, correctly identifying useful species was challenging historically, and confusing one plant for another could be dangerous. To help solve this problem, the University of Padua in northern Italy created the Padua Botanical Garden in 1545. The garden gave scholars a reliable place to study many plants and their therapeutic uses. Its creation became an important step toward safer medical practices and helped establish the organized scientific study of the plant world.

From its earliest years, the Padua Botanical Garden served as a working space for scientific observation. Instead of relying only on drawings, medical students could study living examples. This made identifying medicines safer and more accurate. The garden's directors also began recording information about plants in a more systematic way. They treated plants as complex living organisms rather than just as remedies.

As trade expanded between the Venetian Republic and other parts of the world, opportunities for botanical research expanded with it. Scholars were soon able to study new plant species such as lilacs, sunflowers, and potatoes. This research broadened scientific knowledge and encouraged early attempts at grouping and comparing plants. Because of these advances, the garden became one of the first places in Europe where scientists could study native and foreign species side by side. This work helped lay the foundation for modern botany and pharmacology, the branch of science that studies medicines.

pieces.text: One powerful example of the garden's long-lasting influence is its collection of ancient trees, some of which have been studied for hundreds of years. The most famous is a dwarf fan palm planted in 1585, now called Goethe's Palm, named after the German writer and scientist Johann Wolfgang von Goethe. He visited the garden in 1786 and became fascinated by the tree's changing leaf shapes and impressive age. His observations helped inspire his important work on plant development,
. Today, Goethe's Palm remains one of the garden's best-known features and represents its lasting impact on scientific study.

textContent.text: The garden has continued to grow as a center for research. In 2014, for example, it was enlarged to include the Garden of Biodiversity. This large, climate-controlled greenhouse extends the garden's mission to the study of global plant diversity and environmental change. It displays plants from Earth's major climate zones, such as tropical, temperate, and arid, and it shows how different species adapt to survive in their environments. The exhibits also explain how people throughout history have relied on plants for food, medicine, and materials. By demonstrating the variety of plant life and our dependence on it, the Garden of Biodiversity highlights the importance of protecting Earth's environments.

Although the Padua Botanical Garden has expanded over the centuries, it has kept its historic core. It remains a place for research and education, a shelter for rare and endangered species, and a landmark respected around the world for its major contributions to botanical science.

contents.text: DNA testing is an important tool for identifying and tracking endangered species. For instance, scientists can use DNA to check that fish served in restaurants is correctly labeled. Sometimes, restaurants mistakenly serve endangered fish—periodic DNA tests can help prevent this. But what if the animal in question is still alive? The answer may be eDNA, or environmental DNA, which can be taken from the soil or water in which an animal lives without disturbing the animal itself. Gathering eDNA is less stressful to animals than taking DNA samples, since scientists can simply take samples of water from its environment.

contents.text: DNA testing is an important tool for identifying and tracking endangered species. For instance, scientists can use DNA to check that fish served in restaurants is correctly labeled. Sometimes, restaurants mistakenly serve endangered fish—periodic DNA tests can help prevent this. But what if the animal in question is still alive? The answer may be eDNA, or environmental DNA, which can be taken from the soil or water in which an animal lives without disturbing the animal itself. Gathering eDNA is less stressful to animals than taking DNA samples, since scientists can simply take samples of water from its environment.

contents.text: In lower-income countries, the high cost of medical equipment, such as microscopes, is often an obstacle to providing health care. Stanford University professor Manu Prakash came up with a simple answer: he created Foldscope, a microscope made almost completely of paper that costs less than a dollar. Other equipment, such as centrifuges, needs electricity to operate. Centrifuges spin blood samples to diagnose infections like malaria. To improve health care access in areas without electricity, Prakash invented the Paperfuge. The Paperfuge is a centrifuge made of paper and string. It costs about twenty cents and doesn't require electricity.

contents.text: Were it not for the early conservation efforts, California's national parks may never have come to be. In the 1860s, naturalist John Muir fell in love with California's Yosemite Valley. Alarmed by the damage caused by grazing livestock, he wrote essays to promote the idea of turning the area into protected land. Thanks in part to Muir's writing, Yosemite National Park was created in 1890. Sequoia National Park, established in 1890 by President Benjamin Harrison, was a response to loggers that wanted the area's enormous sequoia trees for lumber. This action effectively shielded many of California's giant sequoias from destruction.

contents.text: Color blindness is a visual impairment that affects how people see one or more colors. Color blindness can make some everyday tasks a bit challenging, such as distinguishing between traffic lights or reading a website. Fortunately, assistive technology offers some great work-arounds. Drivers who are color-blind might consider EnChroma glasses, which help people tell the difference between red and green more easily. What about web designers who want to ensure that their work is color-blind friendly? They can enhance their computer monitors with a color filter to see how their websites appear to color-blind people and make improvements using that knowledge.

contents.text: Before British scientist Alexander Fleming discovered antibiotics in the 1920s, bacterial infections could be deadly. After antibiotics were developed, though, doctors were able to treat infections and save lives. Over the years, however, antibiotics were overused. As a result, antibiotic-resistant bacteria—also known as superbugs—have appeared. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about two million people become infected with superbugs every year. Canadian scientists may have stumbled on a surprising tool to combat the overuse of the drugs. By mixing maple syrup extract with antibiotics, the researchers were able to increase their effectiveness while reducing the dose amount.

contents.text: Saffron and vanilla are the most expensive spices in the world. The vanilla flower is a member of the orchid family. The flowers are difficult to grow, and demand for vanilla is high, so the spice is costly. To avoid the high cost, many consumers purchase imitation vanilla instead. Like vanilla, saffron also comes from a flower—the dried stigmas of a type of crocus flower. To produce one pound of dried saffron, it takes nearly seventy thousand crocus flowers! As a result, saffron is pricey, too. The answer for some consumers is to use inexpensive turmeric in its place.

Stanford University professor Manu Prakash came up with a simple answer: he created Foldscope, a microscope made almost completely of paper that costs less than a dollar. Other equipment, such as centrifuges, needs electricity to operate. Centrifuges spin blood samples to diagnose infections like malaria. To improve health care access in areas without electricity, Prakash invented the Paperfuge. The Paperfuge is a centrifuge made of paper and string. It costs about twenty cents and doesn't require electricity.

contents.text: DNA testing is an important tool for identifying and tracking endangered species. For instance, scientists can use DNA to check that fish served in restaurants is correctly labeled. Sometimes, restaurants mistakenly serve endangered fish—periodic DNA tests can help prevent this. But what if the animal in question is still alive? The answer may be eDNA, or environmental DNA, which can be taken from the soil or water in which an animal lives without disturbing the animal itself. Gathering eDNA is less stressful to animals than taking DNA samples, since scientists can simply take samples of water from its environment.
<instructions>Match the problems with their solutions.</instructions>

Scientists need to study a living animal without causing stress.

contents.text: Were it not for the early conservation efforts, California's national parks may never have come to be. In the 1860s, naturalist John Muir fell in love with California's Yosemite Valley. Alarmed by the damage caused by grazing livestock, he wrote essays to promote the idea of turning the area into protected land. Thanks in part to Muir's writing, Yosemite National Park was created in 1890. Sequoia National Park, established in 1890 by President Benjamin Harrison, was a response to loggers that wanted the area's enormous sequoia trees for lumber. This action effectively shielded many of California's giant sequoias from destruction.

contents.text: Color blindness is a visual impairment that affects how people see one or more colors. Color blindness can make some everyday tasks a bit challenging, such as distinguishing between traffic lights or reading a website. Fortunately, assistive technology offers some great work-arounds. Drivers who are color-blind might consider EnChroma glasses, which help people tell the difference between red and green more easily. What about web designers who want to ensure that their work is color-blind friendly? They can enhance their computer monitors with a color filter to see how their websites appear to color-blind people and make improvements using that knowledge.

contents.text: Like many other countries, Germany produces a huge amount of waste. The German nonprofit group Innatura is trying to change that. Companies often burn perfectly good products simply because promotional offers have ended or packaging has changed. Innatura saves these products from being destroyed. Instead, the group redistributes the products to charities. Food waste is also a big issue in Germany: more than eighteen million metric tons of food are tossed every year. In Berlin, some residents make sure good food doesn't go in the trash. They leave their extras at drop-off points and let others know what's available online.

contents.text: Before British scientist Alexander Fleming discovered antibiotics in the 1920s, bacterial infections could be deadly. After antibiotics were developed, though, doctors were able to treat infections and save lives. Over the years, however, antibiotics were overused. As a result, antibiotic-resistant bacteria—also known as superbugs—have appeared. According to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, about two million people become infected with superbugs every year. Canadian scientists may have stumbled on a surprising tool to combat the overuse of the drugs. By mixing maple syrup extract with antibiotics, the researchers were able to increase their effectiveness while reducing the dose amount.
<instructions>Match the problems with their solutions.</instructions>

staticItems.text: Antibiotics were invented.
Scientists mixed maple syrup with medication.

contents.text: Saffron and vanilla are the most expensive spices in the world. The vanilla flower is a member of the orchid family. The flowers are difficult to grow, and demand for vanilla is high, so the spice is costly. To avoid the high cost, many consumers purchase imitation vanilla instead. Like vanilla, saffron also comes from a flower—the dried stigmas of a type of crocus flower. To produce one pound of dried saffron, it takes nearly seventy thousand crocus flowers! As a result, saffron is pricey, too. The answer for some consumers is to use inexpensive turmeric in its place.
<instructions>Match the problems with their solutions.</instructions>

staticItems.text: Vanilla is expensive.
Saffron is expensive.

contents.text: Saffron and vanilla are the most expensive spices in the world. The vanilla flower is a member of the orchid family. The flowers are difficult to grow, and demand for vanilla is high, so the spice is costly. To avoid the high cost, many consumers purchase imitation vanilla instead. Like vanilla, saffron also comes from a flower—the dried stigmas of a type of crocus flower. To produce one pound of dried saffron, it takes nearly seventy thousand crocus flowers! As a result, saffron is pricey, too. The answer for some consumers is to use inexpensive turmeric in its place.

contents.text: Color blindness is a visual impairment that affects how people see one or more colors. Color blindness can make some everyday tasks a bit challenging, such as distinguishing between traffic lights or reading a website. Fortunately, assistive technology offers some great work-arounds. Drivers who are color-blind might consider EnChroma glasses, which help people tell the difference between red and green more easily. What about web designers who want to ensure that their work is color-blind friendly? They can enhance their computer monitors with a color filter to see how their websites appear to color-blind people and make improvements using that knowledge.

contents.text: DNA testing is an important tool for identifying and tracking endangered species. For instance, scientists can use DNA to check that fish served in restaurants is correctly labeled. Sometimes, restaurants mistakenly serve endangered fish—periodic DNA tests can help prevent this. But what if the animal in question is still alive? The answer may be eDNA, or environmental DNA, which can be taken from the soil or water in which an animal lives without disturbing the animal itself. Gathering eDNA is less stressful to animals than taking DNA samples, since scientists can simply take samples of water from its environment.

contents.text: Were it not for the early conservation efforts, California's national parks may never have come to be. In the 1860s, naturalist John Muir fell in love with California's Yosemite Valley. Alarmed by the damage caused by grazing livestock, he wrote essays to promote the idea of turning the area into protected land. Thanks in part to Muir's writing, Yosemite National Park was created in 1890. Sequoia National Park, established in 1890 by President Benjamin Harrison, was a response to loggers that wanted the area's enormous sequoia trees for lumber. This action effectively shielded many of California's giant sequoias from destruction.

header.text: A clause is a group of words that contains both a subject and predicate. A clause can function as a complete sentence or combine with other clauses to form compound or complex sentences.

sentences.text: Samantha grew up in a bilingual family, so she can speak two languages fluently.
The clause has a subject (she) and a predicate (can speak two languages fluently).
The Hall of Records, which is found behind Mount Rushmore, contains copies of historical United States documents.
The clause has a subject (which) and a predicate (is found behind Mount Rushmore).

header.text: A phrase is any group of words that function together in a sentence but lack a subject, a predicate, or both.

sentences.text: We washed the dishes in the sink after dinner.
The phrase does not contain a subject.
The new physician at the hospital has been working long hours.
The phrase does not contain a predicate.
Robert and Emily took detailed notes during the lecture on microbiology.
The phrase contains neither a subject nor a predicate.
